prompt: What does a first-hop redundancy group give a host?
options: It makes two physical routers use the same real interface IP address.
It guarantees that every remote application stays reachable during any network failure.
It supplies every remote route without a routing protocol or static routes.
It allows another router to assume the shared gateway identity when the current forwarding router fails.
explanation: Hosts use one virtual gateway, and another router takes it over if the forwarding router fails.

whyWrong.0: Each router keeps its own real address; only the virtual address is shared.
whyWrong.1: It protects only the gateway, not every failure.

prompt: What does R2's HSRP status show?
options: R2 is Standby, preemption is configured, and hosts should use 192.168.10.1.
R2 is Active because the Standby column says local.
R2 is Standby, so hosts should use the active real address 192.168.10.2.
R2 is Active because the P flag means preemption has completed.
explanation: R2 is Standby, and the P flag means preemption is configured. Hosts use the virtual IP as their gateway.

whyWrong.1: Local in the Standby column means R2 is the standby.
whyWrong.2: Hosts use the virtual address, not a real one.
whyWrong.3: P means preempt is configured, not that it happened.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R2# show standby brief
Interface Grp Pri P State   Active        Standby Virtual IP
Gi0/0     1   100 P Standby 192.168.10.2  local   192.168.10.1

prompt: Which TWO statements are true of VRRP with non-owner routers and default settings?
options: VRRP is carried in UDP port 1985.
A higher-priority returning router can preempt the current lower-priority router.
The default non-owner priority is 100.
The lower numeric priority is preferred.
VRRPv2 supports IPv6 as well as IPv4.
explanation: The default non-owner priority is 100, and preemption is on by default. VRRP uses IP protocol 112, and VRRPv3 adds IPv6.

whyWrong.3: Higher priority wins.
whyWrong.4: VRRPv2 is IPv4 only; VRRPv3 adds IPv6.

prompt: A VRRP router's real interface address is also the group virtual address. Which priority does it use?
explanation: The VRRP address owner uses priority 255.

whyWrong.2: 254 is the highest priority a non-owner can have.
whyWrong.3: Priority 0 means the router gives up the role.

prompt: What do these VRRPv3 summaries show on R1?
options: R1 forwards for both because both use group number 1.
The IPv6 summary is invalid because VRRP supports only IPv4.
R1 forwards for IPv4 but is Backup for the separate IPv6 instance.
The IPv6 virtual MAC should be changed to the IPv4 virtual MAC.
explanation: IPv4 and IPv6 are separate VRRP instances. R1 is Master for IPv4 and Backup for IPv6.

whyWrong.0: Each address family has its own instance.
whyWrong.3: IPv6 uses its own virtual MAC range.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R1 Group 1, Address-Family IPv4: State Master, VIP 192.168.10.1
R1 Group 1, Address-Family IPv6: State Backup, VIP FE80::1
IPv6 virtual MAC: 0000.5e00.0201

prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts HSRP and VRRP defaults?
options: HSRP preemption is off by default; VRRP preemption is on.
HSRP sends a Hello every second; VRRP advertises every 3 seconds.
HSRP is carried as IP protocol 112; VRRP uses UDP port 1985.
HSRP is an open standard; VRRP is Cisco proprietary.
explanation: HSRP is Cisco proprietary, uses UDP 1985, sends Hellos every 3 seconds and has preemption off. VRRP is a standard, uses IP protocol 112, advertises every 1 second and has preemption on.

whyWrong.3: HSRP is the proprietary one.

prompt: HSRP VIP is .1, R1 is .2 and R2 is .3. A PC uses .2 as its gateway, then R1 fails and R2 becomes Active. What happens?
options: R2 automatically adopts R1's real address .2 as well as the VIP.
The PC still targets the failed real gateway and may lose off-subnet access.
The PC automatically rewrites its static gateway to the advertised virtual address.
The PC keeps .2, but its ARP entry must change to R2 physical MAC for .2.
explanation: The PC still sends to R1's real address, so it loses off-subnet access. Hosts must use the VIP.

whyWrong.0: R2 takes over the virtual identity, not R1's real address.
whyWrong.2: HSRP does not change a host's gateway.
whyWrong.3: R2 does not answer for .2.

prompt: An interface running HSRP version 1 rejects group 300. What must change?
options: Change the virtual IP to another address in the same subnet.
Set standby 300 priority 255 before creating the virtual address.
Change the LAN VLAN number to 300 on the access switch.
Configure standby version 2 on each participating interface.
explanation: HSRPv1 supports groups 0 to 255 and HSRPv2 supports 0 to 4095. Set standby version 2 on both routers.

whyWrong.0: The virtual IP is not the problem.
whyWrong.1: Priority does not extend the group range.
whyWrong.2: The group number is independent of the VLAN.

prompt: R1 recovers with priority 110 but preemption is off. R2 is healthy Active at 100. What happens?
options: R1 must become Active immediately because 110 exceeds 100.
Both routers must become Active because priorities differ.
R2 can remain Active while recovered R1 is Standby.
R2 must disable its LAN interface to release the virtual IP.
explanation: HSRP preemption is off by default, so R2 stays Active and R1 becomes Standby.

whyWrong.3: No interface shutdown is needed.

exhibit.title: Representative R1 show standby excerpt
exhibit.text:
State is Standby
Preemption disabled
Active router is 192.168.10.3, priority 100
Priority 110 (configured 110)

prompt: VRRP R2 is Master at priority 100. Non-owner R1 returns at 110 with default preemption. What happens?
options: R1 must remain Backup because VRRP preemption defaults off.
R2 becomes the address owner because it was Master first.
R1 can preempt R2 and take the forwarding role.
R1 must first change its virtual address to a new subnet.
explanation: VRRP preempts by default and the higher priority wins, so R1 becomes Master.

whyWrong.0: VRRP preemption is on by default.
whyWrong.1: Ownership depends on addresses, not start order.
whyWrong.3: The virtual address must stay the same.

prompt: Which peer forwards in this VRRP owner case?
options: R1, the address owner at priority 255.
R2, because 254 is the highest ordinary non-owner priority.
Whichever non-owner most recently sent an advertisement.
Both peers, because preemption is enabled.
explanation: The address owner uses priority 255, which beats any non-owner (1 to 254). R1 is Master whenever it is up.

whyWrong.3: VRRP has one Master per group.

exhibit.title: VRRP address-owner priorities (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Both peers on the same working LAN, no faults.
R1 real address equals the virtual IPv4 address; priority 255.
R2 real address differs; priority 254; preemption enabled.
Allow protocol processing to settle.

prompt: R1 is Active at priority 100. R2 joins at priority 100 with preempt and a higher real IP. Does R2 preempt?
options: Yes; the IP tiebreaker always preempts an existing Active router.
Yes; preempt forces takeover regardless of priority.
No; R2 must use the same real interface IP as R1.
No; an equal-priority router does not preempt solely because its IP is higher.
explanation: Preemption needs a strictly higher priority. The higher IP only breaks a tie when no Active router exists.

whyWrong.0: The IP address is a tiebreaker only.

prompt: R1 loses its tracked uplink, but R2 (priority 100, preempt) does not take over. Why?
options: R1's effective priority becomes 5, so R2 needs a lower priority.
R1's effective priority falls only to 105, which still exceeds 100.
R2 preempt is irrelevant because it is configured on the standby router.
R1 must reduce its configured priority permanently before tracking can affect it.
explanation: R1's priority drops from 110 to 105 (110 minus 5), which is still above 100. The decrement must take R1 below R2.

whyWrong.0: The decrement is subtracted from the priority, not used as the priority.
whyWrong.2: Preempt on R2 is what allows takeover.
whyWrong.3: Tracking lowers the effective priority automatically.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R1 Gi0/0:
 standby 1 priority 110
 standby 1 preempt
 standby 1 track GigabitEthernet0/1 5
R1 Gi0/1: down/down

prompt: An HSRP Standby has a 10-second hold timer and heard the Active router's last Hello 3 seconds ago. How long until the timer expires?
options: Approximately 7 seconds.
Approximately 3 seconds.
Approximately 10 seconds from now.
Exactly three additional Hello transmissions.
explanation: The hold timer restarts at 10 seconds with each Hello, so 10 minus 3 leaves about 7 seconds.

whyWrong.1: 3 seconds is the time already elapsed.
whyWrong.2: The timer started at the last Hello.
whyWrong.3: The timer counts seconds, not Hellos.

prompt: During HSRP failover, what makes the switch send frames for the virtual MAC to the new Active router?
options: Changing every PC gateway to the new router real IP.
Updating the PC ARP cache alone while leaving the switch MAC location unchanged.
Keeping the old switch port because the virtual gateway IP did not change.
Frames sourced from the virtual MAC, including gratuitous ARP announcements.
explanation: The new Active router sends frames from the virtual MAC, such as a gratuitous ARP. The switch learns the new port from the source MAC.

whyWrong.1: The switch must learn the MAC location itself.
whyWrong.2: The MAC now sits behind a different port.

prompt: Which TWO entries stay unchanged during same-version failover?
options: The switch port learned for the virtual MAC.
The PC configured virtual gateway IP.
The group virtual IP-to-virtual-MAC mapping.
The physical router performing the Active role.
The exact number of application packets lost.
explanation: Hosts keep the virtual gateway IP and its virtual MAC mapping. The switch port and the Active router change.

whyWrong.0: The switch learns the new port.
whyWrong.3: The Active router changes.

prompt: Both routers preempt. R1 has priority 110 for VLAN 10 and 90 for VLAN 20, and R2 has the reverse. What is the steady state?
options: R1 forwards for VLAN 10 while R2 forwards for VLAN 20.
R1 and R2 both forward concurrently for each single HSRP group.
R1 becomes Active for both VLANs because it has a 110 somewhere.
R2 becomes Standby for both VLANs because its VLAN 10 priority is lower.
explanation: Each HSRP group elects its own Active router. R1 forwards for VLAN 10 and R2 for VLAN 20.

whyWrong.1: One router is Active per group.
whyWrong.3: R2 has the higher priority in VLAN 20.

exhibit.title: Representative per-group priority plan
exhibit.text:
VLAN 10 / HSRP group 10: R1 priority 110, R2 priority 90
VLAN 20 / HSRP group 20: R1 priority 90, R2 priority 110
Both routers have preempt enabled in both groups.

prompt: Two HSRP peers each stay Active with an unknown Standby. Which TWO mismatches cause this?
options: Different HSRP versions on the interfaces
Different configured HSRP priorities
Different real interface IPs in the same subnet
Different HSRP group numbers
Preemption enabled on both peers
explanation: Peers must use the same HSRP version and group number. Otherwise they build separate groups.

whyWrong.4: Preempt on both peers does not split the group.

prompt: The virtual gateway answers but the server test fails. Why?
options: R1 remains a reachable first hop but has no usable route to the server prefix.
The PC must change its gateway to R2 real IP whenever a server stops replying.
R2 Standby proves that its physical LAN interface is shut.
An Active HSRP state guarantees that the complete forward and return path works.
explanation: The Active router is a working first hop but has no route to the server. Active describes the gateway role only.

whyWrong.3: Active does not prove the path works.

exhibit.title: Reachable VIP and missing remote route (exercise)
exhibit.text:
PC gateway is the correct VIP 192.168.19.1.
R1 Active, R2 Standby; both LAN interfaces up.
PC ping to VIP succeeds; ping to server 203.0.113.10 fails.
R1 has no covering server route or default after its uplink failure.
No uplink tracking is configured.

prompt: After the tracked failure, what happens, and what must you still check?
options: R2 can preempt R1; remote service still needs separate verification.
R1 stays preferred because its configured priority is still 135.
R1 changes the VIP to its real address because its effective priority fell.
R2 takes over and this alone proves every server is reachable.
explanation: 135 minus 40 is 95, below R2's 110, so R2 preempts. A role change does not prove remote reachability, so test a real destination.

whyWrong.2: Tracking changes priority, not the VIP.
whyWrong.3: A role change does not prove the servers are reachable.

exhibit.title: Tracking state and effective priority (exercise)
exhibit.text:
R1 configured HSRP priority 135; tracked uplink Down; decrement 40.
R1 LAN remains up; R1 is the incumbent Active.
R2 effective priority 110; preemption enabled; uplink healthy.
Both agree on group, version, VIP and VLAN.

prompt: SW1's MAC address table lists 0000.0c07.ac14 on the port toward R2. What does this address identify?
options: The HSRP version 1 virtual MAC for group 20.
The HSRP version 2 virtual MAC for group 14.
The VRRP virtual MAC for IPv4 group 20.
The burned-in MAC of R2's LAN interface.
explanation: 0000.0c07.acXX is the HSRPv1 virtual MAC, and XX is the group in hex: 14 hex is group 20. The switch learned it toward R2, so R2 is Active.

whyWrong.1: HSRPv2 MACs begin 0000.0c9f.f, and 14 is hex for 20.
whyWrong.3: 0000.0c07.ac is reserved for the HSRPv1 virtual MAC.

prompt: Two routers are both Active. What is the next step?
options: Immediately set both real interface addresses to the VIP.
Conclude that preempt must be disabled on both routers.
Compare VLAN reachability, group and version on both peers before naming a specific cause.
Conclude that differing priorities alone caused the split.
explanation: Two Active routers mean the peers do not hear each other. Compare VLAN, version and group on both before choosing a fix.

whyWrong.0: Duplicate addresses cause a new fault.
whyWrong.1: Preempt does not explain the split.
whyWrong.3: Priorities normally differ.

exhibit.title: Two Active peers with incomplete evidence (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Intended HSRP pair:
R1 State Active, Standby unknown
R2 State Active, Standby unknown
No peer configuration comparison or VLAN/control-traffic test has been collected.

prompt: What are the default HSRP Hello and hold timers?
options: 1 second and 3 seconds
3 seconds and 10 seconds
10 seconds and 40 seconds
5 seconds and 15 seconds
explanation: HSRP defaults to a 3-second Hello and a 10-second hold time.

whyWrong.0: 1 second is the VRRP advertisement interval.
whyWrong.2: 10 and 40 are the OSPF Hello and dead defaults.
whyWrong.3: 5 and 15 are not HSRP defaults.

prompt: By default, how much does HSRP interface tracking lower the priority when the tracked object fails?
explanation: The default tracking decrement is 10 unless you set another value.

whyWrong.3: 50 is not the default.

prompt: What are the two HSRP roles that forward and stand by?
options: Master and Backup
Active and Standby
Primary and Secondary
Owner and Member
explanation: HSRP uses Active and Standby. Cisco VRRP output uses Master and Backup.

whyWrong.0: Master and Backup are VRRP terms.
whyWrong.2: Primary and Secondary are not FHRP roles.
whyWrong.3: Owner is a VRRP priority case, not a role pair.

prompt: How is VRRP carried?
options: UDP port 1985
TCP port 179
IP protocol 112
IP protocol 89
explanation: VRRP is carried directly in IP as protocol 112.

whyWrong.3: IP protocol 89 is OSPF.
